O01:
*If you have been here before,* every apple in the bowl has turned a quarter-turn, all together, and the *PRIVATE* door stands wider. Go straight to the choices.

Otherwise: burgundy ground. Gold lozenge. A fern curl. Gold lozenge. Burgundy ground.

The hotel carpet picks up where the skybridge carpet left off, as if you'd only just stepped off it, and carries on. It runs under the reception desk, up the first three stairs and, as far as you can tell, into the walls.

The lobby is low and empty and smells of carpet shampoo. A brass luggage trolley stands by the doors with nothing on it.

On the desk sits a bowl of green apples, every apple turned the same way. Above it hang five clocks labelled with cities that don't exist: *GLASSHAVEN. PORT EVER. SAINT UNDERMERE. HOLLOWMOUTH. LANTERN BAY.* All five have stopped at the same minute.

On the counter: a brass bell, a card that says *PLEASE RING FOR SERVICE*, and a leather guest book lying open with a pen across the page.

*If Sam is with you,* he stops in front of the clocks and reads them one by one, lips moving. He turns his back on them and doesn't look again.

To your left, the lifts, their doors a dull, rubbed gold. To your right, a fire door marked *STAIRS*. At the back, past a velvet rope left to dangle, an amber room where someone is polishing a glass.

Behind the desk, a door marked *PRIVATE* stands ajar. Behind it, something is waiting to be called. It will come if you ring.

If you ring the bell at reception, turn to {O02}.

If you haven't already read the guest book, turn to {O31}.

If you go to the lifts, turn to {O08}.

If you take the stairs, turn to {O12}.

If you haven't already been into the bar, turn to {O26}.
O31:
The guest book is bound in green leather gone soft at the corners. You turn it round to face you.

The columns are ruled in faded red: *NAME. ROOM. DATE.* Every date is the same. *23/11/1998.* Line after line, page after page, in ink gone brown at the edges.

Every name is in different writing. Round schoolroom capitals. A doctor's scrawl. Old-fashioned copperplate that slopes downhill. Someone who pressed so hard the nib tore the paper. You follow the margins down, turning the brittle pages one at a time. The last line is numbered in the same faded red: *137*.

Near the top of the first page, third line down, one signature takes up twice the room of the others. A big confident loop for the C, a flourish underlining the whole thing: the flourish of a man used to signing for things that weigh a great deal.

*Capt. R.*

Your father was Ray. But he printed his name in capitals on everything he ever signed, birthday cards included. You never once saw him loop a letter.

In the *ROOM* column beside it, in the same loop: *Flight deck. A short delay, folks. Thank you for your patience.* It is the Announcer, written down: the calm, unhurried voice from the PA.

*If Sam is with you,* he looks over your shoulder and straightens up. "Loads of people are R," he says. He reaches past you and turns to the back of the book so the line is hidden, and leaves his forearm across it. After a moment he takes it away.

On the last page, below line 137, someone has ruled one more line by hand, unnumbered. It is empty. A fat navy fountain pen lies across it, *NIGHT MANAGER* stamped in gold along the barrel. The cap is off.

Behind the desk, the *PRIVATE* door hasn't moved.

If you ring the bell, turn to {O02}.

If you leave the book and go to the lifts, turn to {O08}.
O02:
*If you have been here before,* he is behind the desk before the bell stops, as if he never left it. Go straight to the choices.

*Ting.*

The note goes on long after you've let go of the bell, thinning out across the lobby until you can't tell if you're hearing it at all.

The door marked *PRIVATE* opens, and the Night Manager comes through it. And keeps coming.

He has to stoop under the frame. Straightened up behind the desk, his head is nearer the ceiling than it is to you. Larkvale navy, a 1998 cut, red piping at the cuffs. A brass badge, *NIGHT MANAGER*, the letters polished soft. Outside his tie, on a fine steel chain, hangs a wedding ring.

He doesn't smile. He has the patient, creased face of a man four hours into a twelve-hour shift.

"Good evening," he says. "Checking in?"

You can't hold his look for long. You look down at the brass kickplate along the front of the desk, polished to a mirror. It shows the lobby behind you. The trolley. The apples. Your own pale face.

It doesn't show him. The desk, the wall behind the desk, and in between, nobody at all.

*If Sam is with you,* he's seen it too. He doesn't step back. "Ask him," he says, barely moving his lips. "About my passport. Go on."

"We have rooms," the Night Manager says, "if you need to rest." On the last word his eyes go, just once, to the lifts.

If you haven't already checked in, and you want to, turn to {O03}.

If you ask about lost passports, turn to {O05}.

If you back away from the desk and make for the lifts, turn to {O08}.
O03:
"Lovely." The Night Manager opens a leather ledger, runs one long nail down to an empty line, and uncaps a pen.

"Name for the booking?"

And you give it. You don't decide to. It's the middle of the night, a man in a uniform has asked you a question you've answered in a hundred hotels, and your mouth does what it always does, and gives him your name.

The pen scratches. It scratches for longer than your name should take.

Add 1 to your Claim.

He slides a key card across the desk. White, gold stripe, small neat capitals: *ROOM 1952*.

It takes you a second. Nineteen fifty-two. The year the old terminal opened. The year Dad was born.

*If Sam is with you,* he picks up the card, turns it over, and puts it down again. "That's not funny," he tells the Night Manager.

The Night Manager blots the ledger and closes it.

"Checkout is by six," he says. "You'll want to be well rested."

Note the ROOM KEY on your Adventure Sheet, and note the codeword CHECKED IN.

Behind him, in the wooden pigeonholes for guests' messages, a folded white slip sits in the slot marked 1952. When you look again the slot is empty, and he hasn't moved.

Turn to {O08}.
O05:
*If you have asked before,* he only inclines his head towards the safe. Go straight to the choices.

"Lost property." The Night Manager says it with real sorrow. "So much goes astray on a night like this."

He inclines his head towards an alcove beside the desk. In it squats an old green safe, waist high, with a modern keypad bolted to its door.

"Anything a guest has mislaid is kept in the safe," he says. "Anything that's been handed in."

"And the code?"

He looks at you for a while before he answers. In the brass kickplate below him, the space behind the desk stands empty.

"The code is the year someone you lost was born."

He says it kindly, like a quizmaster giving a clue, and then he lets the quiet do the asking. He has had practice.

*If Sam is with you,* he opens his mouth. "How does he…" He doesn't finish. He looks at the safe, then at you, and folds his arms.

On the keypad a small screen glows green. Four empty boxes, side by side.

If you try the safe, turn to {O06}.

If you thank him, back away, and head for the lifts, turn to {O08}.
O06:
You crouch in front of the safe. Up close it smells of old metal and, under that, of the inside of a handbag: face powder, peppermints, pennies. The green paint has worn through to grey around the handle where a great many people have pulled at it.

Four empty boxes. Beneath them, on a strip of yellowed label tape: *YEAR OF BIRTH*.

Someone you lost. You think of a man on a viewing deck with a paper cup of tea, and a firm grip on the hood of your anorak so you couldn't lean too far over the rail. *Where are they going, then?*

At your back, you can feel the Night Manager not moving.

*If Sam is with you,* he crouches beside you. His knees crack. "Don't get it wrong," he says. "I don't think we're allowed to get it wrong."

You hesitate over the first key. Somewhere behind the walls, a bell rings once and stops.

If you know the year, subtract 1800 from it and turn to the section with that number. If you don't, guess: tap in any four digits you like and turn to {O07}.
SAFE:
The keypad gives a small, satisfied chirp. The screen turns from green to gold.

Inside the door, a bolt draws back with a heavy clunk, and the safe swings open on its own, slowly, then all the way, on hinges that haven't been oiled since before you were born.

When you glance back, the Night Manager is watching the safe, not you.

Inside, on a shelf lined with green felt, are two things.

The first is a burgundy passport, bent at one corner where it was shoved into a backpack this morning. You open it. Sam at twenty-six, scowling at a photo booth. Note the PASSPORT on your Adventure Sheet.

The second is a wristwatch. Steel, scratched, on a leather strap worn to the shape of a wrist you would know anywhere. It has stopped at 05:59.

You pick it up. It's warm. And it isn't his. His watch is in a padded envelope at the funeral home, with his wedding ring and his reading glasses, waiting for one of you to sign for it. This is a copy, true to the last scratch. You put it back on the felt.

*If Sam is with you,* he reaches past you and touches the watch face. "He wound it every morning," he says. "Twelve turns, and he counted every one." He stands. "Thanks. For remembering."

As the door swings shut, the watch ticks. Once. Forwards.

Turn to {O19}.
O07:
The screen flashes red. For a second nothing else happens, and you have time to think, *oh, that's all right, then*.

Then the siren starts: an old two-tone wail, rising and falling, the sound of an air raid in a black-and-white film. Every lamp in the lobby turns red. The apples rock in their bowl.

Behind the desk, the Night Manager unfolds.

There's no other word for it. You were sure he was already at his full height, but there is more of him.

He rises joint by joint, a carpenter's rule opening, until his head is bent sideways against the ceiling so he can keep looking at you. His tie swings out and turns slowly in the red light.

"Oh dear," he says over the siren, entirely pleasant. "Oh dear. That wasn't it at all."

He leans his long weight on the desk and begins to come over it. He doesn't hurry. He doesn't need to.

*If Sam is with you,* he's already hauling you up by the back of your jacket. "Lifts," he says. "Lifts. Now."

If you stand your ground and fight him, turn to {O20}.

If you run for the lifts, turn to {O08}.
O08:
*If you have been here before,* the lift is there ahead of you, doors open. Go straight to the choices.

The lift is there when you reach it, doors already open, as if it heard you coming.

Inside: a small mirrored box, a brass rail, the same burgundy-and-gold carpet, and that lift smell of dust and someone else's perfume. You step in. Whatever was behind you, the doors close on it without a sound.

You look at the buttons.

They begin where buttons begin. A round *B*, with a handwritten card taped beside it: *LAUNDRY. STAFF ONLY.* Above it, *0*. *1, 2, 3, 4*.

After that they climb, a brass column from your knee to above your head, each button smaller than the last, until at the top there is one number so long it's only a line of tiny marks. Your eyes won't stay on it.

The *0* is different. Its brass is worn hollow, polished pale by someone who pressed it again and again. Somebody came back to that floor every day.

*If Sam is with you,* he looks at the hollow for a moment, fits his thumb into it without pressing, and takes it away again.

In the mirrored walls, a hundred copies of you stand in the lift. The furthest ones, small and far back, aren't standing quite as you are.

If you press 4 and you haven't already pressed it tonight, turn to {O30}.

If you press 4 and you have pressed it before, turn to {O09}.

If you press 0, turn to {O10}.

If you press B, for the basement laundry, turn to {O15}.

If you step back out into the lobby, turn to {O01}.
O30:
The lift rises. 1, 2, 3. A soft chime, and the doors open on Floor 4.

You step out onto the burgundy carpet. Behind you, the doors slide shut.

Above them runs a row of little amber numbers. The *4* goes dark. The *3* lights. *2*. *1*. *0*, and there it stays, long enough that your shoulders come down.

Something down there has called the lift.

The *1* lights. The *2*. The *3*.

*If Sam is with you,* he watches the numbers with his jaw set. When the *3* lights, he takes one step back from the doors, then another, an arm out behind him feeling for the wall.

*4.* The chime. The doors open.

The tall passenger is inside, folded to fit. Its head is bent against the ceiling, its knees drawn up, the long coat creased across itself in more places than a coat should crease. There's no room to raise its sign, so it holds it against its chest.

The sign carries one letter for every point of your Claim: the first letters of your name. If your Claim is 0, the card is blank, and it holds it anyway.

Its shoulders aren't level. The left sits higher than the right. As you watch, they change places.

The corridor lights begin to flicker. Gain 1 Fear.

Off. On. Off. Each time they come back, the doors are open, and it is there, and it hasn't moved. Not while you're looking.

If you hold its gaze until the doors close on it, knowing it is learning your face, add 1 to your Claim and turn to {O09}.

If you shut your eyes and back away down the corridor, listening to the coat move in the dark, gain 2 more Fear and turn to {O09}.
O09:
*If you have been here before,* the static swells to meet you. Go straight to the choices.

Static.

A television hiss behind every door in the corridor, dozens of them, all tuned to the same nothing. It swells and fades together, and you find you've been breathing in time with it.

The corridor is long and dim, wide enough for two walking side by side. Doors run down both walls: dark wood, brass numbers, a peephole in each. The numbers aren't in order. 412. 1998. 4. 137. 412 again. The carpet carries its pattern away into the distance and doesn't bother to end.

Halfway along, in an alcove under a stuttering strip light, an ice machine hums. Back at the lifts, the little amber number above the doors reads *4*, and holds.

You walk. You stop. The static stops half a second after you.

*If Sam is with you,* he walks ahead, trying each door handle as he passes. "412. Again. Great." *If you also have TRUCE,* he drops back level with you after a while. "I'm not doing these on my own," he says.

Somewhere down the corridor, behind one door among all the doors, the static clears for a second, and an audience laughs at a joke you didn't hear, and it's hiss again.

If you have the ROOM KEY, you can find Room 1952: turn to {O11}.

If you haven't already knocked on one of these doors, choose one at random and knock: turn to {O13}.

If you haven't already been to the ice machine, turn to {O27}.

If you'd rather go back to the lifts, turn to {O08}.
O10:
*If you have been here before,* the monitor hasn't missed a beat. Go straight to the choices.

The lift doors open on a smell before anything else.

Alcohol gel. Overboiled vegetables from a trolley somewhere. And under them, faint and impossible, his aftershave: the green bottle on the bathroom shelf.

There's no corridor. The lift opens straight into a room.

A hospital room. A bed with railings, angled up. A monitor on a jointed arm, beeping, slow and patient. A window with the blind half down and orange car-park light through the slats. A whiteboard by the door: *PATIENT*, *VISITORS*, *YOUR NURSE TODAY IS*, the names rubbed out.

A get-well card from the darts club. A high-backed visitor's chair, its cushion sat thin.

On a hook on the back of the door hangs a long grey wool coat.

You have never been in this room. You saw it once, in the corner of a video call, for four minutes, before you said the signal was going.

Someone is in the bed. The blanket rises and falls. A big-knuckled hand lies on top of it, a plaster on the back where the drip went in, its fingertips resting on a small burgundy book on the bedside table. A passport.

*If Sam is with you,* he steps out of the lift ahead of you. He doesn't look at the bed. He checks the monitor, the drip stand, the chart clipped to the rail, in order, a round he has walked a few hundred times. He puts himself between you and the bed, and his voice has changed, each word set down where he wants it: the voice of a man who has spelled Dad's surname to a great many receptionists. "Right. That's the chip in the windowsill. That's the card from the darts lads. That's not him. Don't. Don't sit in that chair."

*If Sam is with you,* his hand goes to the backpack, to the carrier bag inside it, and stays there.

The head on the pillow begins, slowly, to turn towards you.

If you go in and sit with him, turn to {O14}.

If you step back into the lift and let it carry you up to Floor 4, turn to {O09}.
O14:
You sit. The visitor's chair takes your weight with a sigh of vinyl. The cushion is worn to somebody else's shape.

The head on the pillow finishes turning.

It's him. The jowls he got in his sixties. The eyebrows gone wild. The nick on his chin from shaving once he had started to shake. Thinner, so much thinner than three years ago, when he stood on the front step and gave you one quick salute as Sam's car pulled away.

"There you are," he says. The burr in it. The cough behind the words. *If you have FORGOT,* you know the words, the way they always went; the sound of them is gone, and you take the burr on trust.

"Stay a while." The hand on the passport doesn't move. "You didn't, last time."

Then it says your name. Not the one he called you.

Its chest rises. The monitor beeps. Its chest falls. The two are not keeping time.

"Four months I kept it from you," it says gently. "So you wouldn't worry. And you didn't, did you?"

*If you are his son:* "Stay with your old dad, lad." *If you are his daughter:* "Stay with your old dad, girl." *If neither:* "Stay with your old dad, kid."

Your chest locks. You can't get air past it. You're gripping the arms of the chair, shaking, and you can't make it stop.

*If Sam is with you,* he's crouched in front of you before you've finished breaking, his back to the bed, his elbows on his own knees, an inch from yours. "Kite," he says. Not loud. "Look at me. Breathe when I do." He breathes for both of you, slow and audible, until you catch up. *If you also have TRUCE,* two of his fingers rest on the pulse in your wrist. When you can see again he says, "He told me first. Made me swear not to ring you. Four months, I kept it. We can fight about that later. Passport. Then the lift. I've got the doors."

Slowly, the room comes back.

The fingers on the passport tighten. The monitor slows, waiting to hear what you'll do.

If you have the codeword TOLD, you know what this room is for, and what you came here to say: turn to {O16}.

If you do not, you'll have to take the passport from under that hand and get out: turn to {O17t}.
O16:
You stand up. The chair wants you back. The voice wants you; it is saying your name again, softly. You turn your back on the bed.

He isn't in it. If he's anywhere in this room, he's on the back of the door, in a grey wool coat that still holds the shape of his shoulders, one button sewn on in the wrong colour.

You touch the sleeve. Aftershave. Cold air. The mints he kept in the pocket.

"Hi, Dad," you say. "Sorry I'm late."

You said the worst of it out loud once already tonight. What's left is smaller, and older.

"You should have told me. Four months."

The coat says nothing.

"I'd have come." You stop. "I don't know if I'd have come."

You stay like that until you're sure that's all of it.

"Bye, Dad."

The monitor doesn't flatline. It stops, the way a machine stops when someone is finally allowed to switch it off.

Behind you, the thing in the bed lets out a long breath. When you turn, the blanket is sinking. It settles, and there is no one under it.

*If Sam is with you,* he's at the foot of the bed. For a while he doesn't say anything. He sits in the visitor's chair, his chair, and smooths the empty blanket. "He'd have said you took your time," he says, and his voice goes, and so does yours when you laugh.

*If you have the codeword LOST,* cross it off: Sam is asleep in a second visitor's chair in the corner, one you'd swear wasn't there when you sat down, under a hospital blanket. You shake him until he wakes and says, "You came." Note the codeword TRUCE.

The passport lies on the bedside table, let go of at last. Note the PASSPORT on your Adventure Sheet. Lose 3 Fear.

The lift doors stand open behind you. Nothing is coming through them, and nothing is going to.

Turn to {O19}.
O17t:
You don't answer it. You don't trust your voice not to. You get to your feet and reach for the passport instead.

It lies half under his knuckles. As you touch the cover, the hand turns over, slowly, and lies open beside it, palm up. The way Dad's lay on the arm of his chair during the news, when he wanted one of you to hold it and would never have said so.

"Just a minute," says his voice. "Sit with me just a minute."

The chair is behind your knees. Your legs have been asking all night for someone to tell them they can stop.

*If Sam is with you,* he has backed off to the lift doors, and his voice comes from there, close and calm: "Passport. Then eyes on me, not on the bed."

Test your Nerve. If you succeed, turn to {O17}. If you fail, turn to {D06}.
O17:
You snatch it. The passport comes away. The fingers on the bedside table snap shut on the air where it was, and the blanket heaves. For one second it lifts, and you see a shoulder where no shoulder should be, down by the foot of the bed, turning towards you under the sheet.

"Stay," says Dad's voice. It doesn't shout. It says your name, and says it again, and is still saying it as you back into the lift and slap the panel.

*If Sam is with you,* he's already inside, jamming the door button, jaw clenched. He watches the bed through the narrowing gap.

Gain 2 Fear. Note the PASSPORT on your Adventure Sheet.

The doors close slowly. The last thing you see through the narrowing gap is the head on the pillow, turned towards you, still saying your name to the space where you were.

Turn to {O19}.
D06:
You sit back down.

Just for a minute. Your legs have carried you since the other airport, the other country, the last three years. The vinyl takes your weight and holds it.

The hand finds yours on the blanket. Warm. Exactly the right size.

"There," says his voice. "That's better."

Behind you, the lift doors close. If anyone calls your name from inside, you don't hear it. You meant to do something about the doors. You'll think what in a minute.

The monitor beeps. The orange light through the blind never changes. You hold on, and you sit, and you sit. Visiting hours on Floor 0 don't end.

Much later, weeks or years, someone in navy with red piping comes in to update the whiteboard. They rub out the old name with a sleeve. Under *PATIENT*, in neat capitals, they write yours.

Under *VISITORS*, they write nothing. Nobody comes.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {O10} and choose again.
O11:
The key card clicks. A small green light, and the door of Room 1952 swings inward on a waft of lavender.

It's a lovely room. That's the first wrong thing. After the corridor and the static it is genuinely lovely: lamps lit, curtains drawn, the bed turned down in a crisp white triangle. The television shows a soft blue screen and the word *WELCOME*, with no name after it. It's quiet enough to hear the lamps.

On the pillow, square in the centre, lies Sam's passport.

*If Sam is with you,* he stops in the doorway and comes no further. He looks at the passport for a long moment, then at the bed. "Don't sit on it," he says. "Whatever you do."

*If you have the codeword LOST,* Sam is asleep in the bed, earbuds in, the sheet tucked across his chest in hospital corners. He doesn't stir when you say his name.

Your whole body aches. When did you last sleep? On the plane, a little. Not since. Checkout isn't until six. A minute couldn't hurt. Sit on the edge. Take your shoes off. Let your eyes close, only for a moment.

On the far side of the bed, the covers are turned back too. Waiting.

If you take the passport and go, waking Sam first if he's here, turn to {O18}.

If you lie down for a minute first, turn to {D07}.
O18:
You don't let yourself sit. You don't look at the bed any longer than it takes to lift the passport off the pillow. Note the PASSPORT on your Adventure Sheet.

*If you have the codeword LOST,* cross it off and note the codeword TRUCE: you rip the hospital corners loose and shake Sam awake. He sees the sheet in your fists and says, "You came back."

Out in the corridor, the door clicks shut behind you. Through it, the mattress creaks. Someone getting up. Or lying down.

*If Sam was already with you,* he doesn't speak until you're both at the lifts. *If you also have TRUCE,* he takes the passport, opens it at his own photo, and laughs, not steadily. "Why was my passport on the pillow like a mint." He gives it back. "You keep it. I'll only lose it again."

Turn to {O19}.
D07:
Just a minute.

You sit on the edge of the bed, and then you're lying down, and you don't remember the part in between. The mattress takes you in. The pillow smells of clean cotton and, faintly, of Dad's aftershave.

If anyone is saying your name from the doorway, it's a long way off. You'll answer in a minute.

Out in the corridor, a trolley squeaks. Squeak, squeak, the wheel every hotel trolley has. It stops outside your door.

A gentle knock. "Turndown service."

You'd swear you locked the door. It opens anyway.

You can't lift your head. At the edge of your eye: navy, red piping, a brass badge polished soft. Long fingers fold the sheet across your chest. Tuck it. Tuck it tighter. Hospital corners. They smooth the edges until the shape under the covers is neat, and small, and doesn't move.

"Well rested," says the Night Manager.

In the morning, Room 1952 is immaculate. On the outside of the door hangs a little card: *DO NOT DISTURB*.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {O09} and choose again.
O12:
The fire door sighs shut behind you. Concrete, the hum of strip lights, the cold coming off painted breeze-block.

You start down. Your footsteps ring, and half a beat later the stairwell rings them back.

Each landing has a number stencilled on the wall in red. *B1.* Down a flight. *B2.* Down a flight. *B3.*

Down a flight.

*B3.*

You stop. The same red stencil. The same drip of paint off the foot of the numeral. The same fire extinguisher, the same cigarette burn on the handrail, a black crescent you touched thirty seconds ago.

Below you the stairs keep going down into a damp, soapy dark, and you can hear machines turning over and over.

*If Sam is with you,* he touches the burn. "We've done this one," he says. "I touched this." He looks at you. "The Handbook. Number seven. What did it say?"

Somewhere below, a voice says a word you can't make out. The stairwell gives it back half a second late, and wrong.

If you decide this is wrong and turn back up the stairs, turn to {O08}.

If you keep going down, turn to {O15}.

If you have the TORCH, shine it on the sign. In its beam the red *B3* runs like wet paint, and behind it there's no number at all, only bare wall, breathing in and out. The signs are wrong. You climb back up, fast, and come out beside the lifts: turn to {O08}.
O13:
You pick a door. No reason. 412, or 1998, or none; the brass number swims when you look at it straight. You knock.

The static behind it stops.

The door swings open by itself, and you're looking into your childhood bedroom.

Yours, to the last detail. The wallpaper with the hot-air balloons, one corner peeling where you picked at it every night. The bunk beds. A paper kite hanging from the ceiling on fishing line, turning slowly in a draught that isn't there. A moon-shaped nightlight, glowing.

*If Sam is with you,* he looks at the bunks and his mouth goes thin. "They went to the charity shop," he says. "When I moved back in to look after him. I slept on a camp bed in here." He doesn't look at you. "You'd have known that, if you'd…" The rest stays in his mouth.

The duvet on the bottom bunk is flung back, the sheet still creased from someone's weight.

There's a dull glint under the bottom bunk, just where the nightlight gives out. You get down on your knees on the carpet you built forts on, and you reach into the dark.

Test your Fortune. If you are Lucky, turn to {O22}. If you are Unlucky, turn to {O23}.
O22:
You touch cold metal with a dent in the lid, and you know what it is before you've pulled it out.

Your old first-aid tin. A biscuit tin, really, tartan, a Scottie dog on the lid, that Dad filled with plasters and antiseptic and a roll of bandage the year you were seven and announced you'd be a doctor. You'd forgotten it existed. When you open it, everything inside is new.

Note the FIRST-AID KIT on your Adventure Sheet. Once, at any time, you may open it to restore 6 Vigour (never above its starting score), then cross it off.

*If Sam is with you,* he looks at it, then away. "He kept that in the bathroom cabinet," he says. "Twenty-seven years." A pause. "You put a plaster on my knee out of that once. Sticky side up. I wore it a week so you wouldn't find out."

When you stand, the nightlight goes out. In the dark, the bottom bunk creaks under a weight. You leave without looking back. The door shuts behind you on its own, and the static starts again.

Turn to {O09}.
O23:
You touch something cool and smooth in the dark. Metal, you think.

Then it closes around your wrist.

Fingers. Small ones, a child's, and then not a child's, because there are too many of them, and they grip with no idea how hard is too hard. It pulls. You're dragged forward on your stomach across the carpet until your face is at the edge of the dark under the bed, and the dark is breathing.

*If Sam is with you,* he grabs your ankles and hauls with everything he has, swearing at you, at it, at the wallpaper.

Your wrist tears free. You lie on the carpet, gasping. Lose 3 Vigour.

Round your wrist there's a ring of small round bruises, too many of them, too close together.

You scramble back out into the corridor. From under the bed, a giggle. The static swallows it as the door swings shut.

Turn to {O09}.
O27:
The ice machine hums in its alcove. Above it, the strip light stutters. A sign: *ICE: FOR GUEST USE ONLY*. A plastic scoop on a little chain.

You don't need ice. You need to do one ordinary thing. You press the lever.

The machine shudders. Ice rattles into the tray, and you look down, and each cube has teeth in it.

Small ones. Milk teeth, white, frozen at the heart of the ice. Two or three in some. In one, a whole crescent of them, still set in gum. The machine doesn't stop. The tray fills and overflows, cubes skitter across the carpet, clicking, and still it keeps coming. Gain 1 Fear.

*If Sam is with you,* he clamps on to your arm. He's shaking, all of him, teeth chattering. He isn't looking at the ice any more. He's looking at you.

The ice keeps coming. Under the clatter, from the wall behind the machine, comes small frightened breathing that catches in hitches.

If you stay where you are until it passes, turn to {O28}.

If you back away and keep walking, turn to {O09}.
O28:
You hold on, and let the machine do what it wants.

*If Sam is with you,* you put your arms round him. He goes rigid, then grips your jacket in both fists and puts his forehead on your shoulder. *If you also have THAW or TRUCE,* he answers the question you haven't asked yet: "I'm all right. Give me a minute." When he steps back, he wipes his face. "Don't," he says. You don't.

*If you have the codeword LOST,* you press your ear to the wall and hum the tune Dad hummed in the car. Faint, through the plaster, someone hums it back, flat and tuneless and a beat behind. Sam. You'd know his version anywhere. Whatever is between you now, it isn't only a wall.

The machine empties itself and the carpet darkens with meltwater, and it clicks off. In the tray one last cube is melting, and the little teeth inside it have settled into the shape of a smile.

Note the codeword TRUCE.

Turn to {O09}.
O15:
*If you have been here before,* the folders are still folding. Go straight to the choices.

Heat hits you first, then the noise.

The laundry is enormous. Too big for any hotel, any basement: a low concrete hall lit by caged bulbs, running away into steam until you can't see the end.

Rows of machines with round glass doors, every one of them turning, and behind every porthole navy cloth tumbles over and over. Red piping. Sleeves, collars, the wink of a brass badge going round.

Larkvale uniforms. Hundreds of them. Thousands.

Down the middle of the hall run long steel tables, and at the tables the staff are folding.

They stand in a line with their backs to you. Fold, smooth, fold, stack. Every pair of arms moves at the same instant. Nobody speaks. Now and then one of them holds a jacket up against its own chest, measuring, and lays it on the pile.

Near you stands a rail of fresh-pressed uniforms in plastic, and beside it a tall laundry trolley heaped with sheets, deep enough to hide in.

*If Sam is with you,* he leans close. "Either we wear one of those," he murmurs, "or we get in that." A beat. "I vote that. I've seen films."

At the nearest table, one of the folders stops folding. Its head begins to turn towards you. It keeps turning after a head should stop.

If you do not already have the UNIFORM, and you slip one off the rail, turn to {O24}.

If you climb into the laundry trolley and pull the sheets over you, turn to {O25}.
O24:
You lift one off the rail. The plastic crackles. None of the other folders turns.

You pull the jacket on over your clothes. You need your arms free, and there's nowhere else to put it.

The shoulders sit on your shoulders. The cuffs stop at your wrists. Over the breast pocket there's a brass name badge, blank, waiting to be engraved. The cloth smells of starch, and under the starch, faintly, of someone who wore it for a long time.

Gain 1 Fear. Note the UNIFORM on your Adventure Sheet.

*If Sam is with you,* he looks at you in it for a second too long. "Suits you," he says. Neither of you laughs.

In the porthole of the nearest machine your reflection looks back in navy and red piping. It's smiling. You aren't.

At the table, the folder that turned has put down its jacket and stepped out of the line. You do the only thing left. You dive into the laundry trolley and drag the sheets over your head. *If Sam is with you,* he's already in there, knees up, making room.

Turn to {O25}.
O25:
*If you have been here before,* it is the same two voices, the same conversation, word for word. They laugh in the same place. Turn to {O01}.

Otherwise: dark. Cotton. The smell of hot sheets and starch.

You lie curled in the bottom of the trolley with linen heaped over you, breathing through your mouth.

The trolley begins to move. One wheel squeaks. You're pushed down the hall, round a corner, up a ramp. Two sets of footsteps walk beside you in step, and two voices talk over the top of the sheets, mild and pleasant, staff near the end of a long night.

"The captain says the seat's been empty twenty-eight years."

"Long time to keep a seat. And the gentleman won't be joining us now."

"No. He's gone where we can't book him."

"Children'll do. Guests are always found where they sleep."

They laugh, both at once, the same laugh.

*If Sam is with you,* he's folded in beside you, knees in your back, and at *children* he goes rigid. *If you also have TRUCE,* he says into the dark by your ear, barely aloud: "They're not having you either."

The trolley stops. The footsteps walk away, still in step. When you climb out, blinking, there's burgundy and gold under your feet again.

Turn to {O01}.
O26:
The bar smells of beer mats and furniture polish.

Low amber lamps. Leather stools. Bottles lined up behind the counter, lit from beneath. A piano in the corner with its lid shut.

No other drinkers, but there are glasses on some of the tables, half finished, the ice in them not melted, as though a whole room of people stood up a moment ago and left in the same direction.

The bartender wears a Larkvale waistcoat with red piping. He's polishing a glass, the one you saw from the lobby. The cloth has worn through in the middle, and his skin is pink and shiny where it rubs. He doesn't stop polishing to serve you.

He builds the drink one-handed without looking: whisky, ginger ale, two cubes of ice, a twist of lime. He slides it across on a paper coaster.

Dad's drink. Weddings, Christmas, one night a year at the darts club.

"On the house," says the bartender.

The glass sweats. You can smell it from here, sharp and sweet. Your tongue is sticking to your teeth. When did you last drink anything? The clock over the till says a little past midnight. Everything in here says a little past midnight.

*If Sam is with you,* he looks at the glass, then at you. "That's his," he says. "That's his actual drink." A pause. "The Handbook had a rule about this." He doesn't say which. He wants to see if you remember.

If you drink it, turn to {O29}.

If you leave it on the bar and walk out, turn to {O01}.
O29:
You drink it. Warmth unfolds in your chest, runs down your arms, loosens your fists, which you realise have been clenched for hours. Your legs are your own again. Gain 3 Vigour.

It tastes of the one sip he let you have at your aunt's wedding when you were twelve, with a wink: *don't tell your mother*.

The bartender takes the empty glass and writes on a little pad. He tears off the page and pushes it down onto a brass spike beside the till, on top of a great many other little pages. Years of them. The ones at the bottom have gone the yellow of old teeth. Note the codeword FED.

"I'll put that on your tab," he says.

"You said it was on the house."

"It is." He begins to polish your glass. "You're in the house."

*If Sam is with you,* he doesn't say *I told you*. He looks at the spike of little pages for a long moment, and walks out ahead of you and doesn't wait.

The taste stays. Under the lime, faintly, old coins.

All the way back across the lobby, you can hear the bartender polishing your glass.

Turn to {O01}.
O19:
The lobby lets you through without a word: past the bell, past the apples, out through the far doors onto the skybridge.

It is a long glass tube slung across the dark between the hotel and the terminal, carpeted in the same burgundy and gold, so the pattern follows you out. Beyond the glass there's nothing. No runway lights, no car parks, no planes. Black, and your reflection keeping pace on the other side.

The passport is in your inside pocket. You keep touching it to check.

*If Sam is with you,* he keeps to the middle of the carpet and doesn't look out. "Not one plane," he says. "Not one light." *If you also have TRUCE,* "Where are they going, then?" you say across the carpet, and he answers as quick as he did at five: "Lantern Bay." He laughs, and the laugh runs away down the glass and comes back right.

*If you have the codeword CHECKED IN,* a voice calls after you from the lobby you've left behind. Pleasant. Unhurried. Carrying the length of the glass. *"Checkout by six."* You don't turn round.

Ahead, through the doors at the end of the skybridge, the terminal's lights come up to meet you, and the great departures board ticks over with that soft clatter you used to love.

You go on, back towards the Atrium.

Tick one hour on your Adventure Sheet.

If you have just ticked your sixth hour, turn to {E_FINALCALL}.

If you do not have RETURNED, turn to {H05}.

If you have RETURNED but not HEARD, turn to {H03}.

Otherwise turn to {H01}.
O20:
You don't run. You've been running for three years and you're tired of the view. You plant your feet on the burgundy carpet and put your fists up as Dad showed you in the back garden, thumbs outside, chin down.

The Night Manager comes over the desk the way a spider comes over the rim of a bath, all joints and patience.

He gets your collar, cold and dry and far stronger than he looks, and lifts you onto your toes. You hit his wrist. Something in it gives with a crack of snapping twigs, and the grip doesn't loosen at all.

"There's no need for a fuss," he says. "You can rest." He bends closer, to say it gently.

That's your opening. You drive your fist into the brass badge and feel your knuckles split on it. Up close he smells of starch and cold air and an old man's hair oil.

*If Sam is with you,* he rams the brass luggage trolley into the backs of the Night Manager's knees, hard enough to fold them.

NIGHT MANAGER   NERVE 9   VIGOUR 10

If you win, turn to {O21}.

If your Vigour reaches 0, turn to {D_VIGOUR}.
O21:
The Night Manager goes down joint by joint, folding in on himself until he's lying behind the desk in a heap far too small for him. The siren winds down. The lamps fade back to amber.

His brass badge has come off. It lies on the carpet by your shoe. You pick it up. On the back, scratched in with a pin and worn almost smooth: *Home by Tuesday. J.*

You set it on the desk, beside the bell.

His leather ledger lies open, knocked crooked in the struggle. The columns are ruled in faded red. *NAME. ROOM. ARRIVED. DEPARTED.* The *DEPARTED* column is empty all the way down, page after page.

*If you have the codeword CHECKED IN,* the last line on the last page is yours. Your name, in your own handwriting, though you never touched the pen. *ROOM 1952.* The *DEPARTED* box is waiting.

Tucked inside the back cover, pressed shut by the weight of all those names, is a burgundy passport. Sam's. Note the PASSPORT on your Adventure Sheet.

*If Sam is with you,* he takes it, checks the photo, checks it again. "Thank you," he says. He looks at your split knuckles. "You punched a hotel manager." A beat. "I've wanted to hit something since the funeral home rang."

Behind the desk, the heap that was the Night Manager is breathing. Slowly. And getting longer.

Turn to {O19}.
